newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: "Red Vienna" seen turning its back on socialism.
newsitem.headline: "Red Vienna" seen turning its back on socialism.

text.p: Austrian Social Democrats look set to lose their grip on the city known for generations as "Red Vienna" in state polls that could have implications for the entire country.
Vienna, a hotbed of civil unrest in the 1920s, has been a socialist stronghold for most of the century, eclipsed only by Austrian fascist and German Nazi rule between 1934 and 1945.
Political analysts say the October 13 election, which coincides with a European parliamentary poll, will focus on jobs, foreigners and welfare.
"Emotions are running high over the number of foreigners in Vienna because people believe they take away jobs and social payments," said Werner Beutelmeyer of Linz-based research institute Market.
In some districts, immigrants from ex-Yugoslavia, eastern Europe and Turkey make up about a third of the population. In the city as a whole, foreigners account for 18.4 percent of the population.
The far-right Freedom Party has capitalised on fears of unemployment and the rising resentment over an influx of immigrants and refugees from former Yugoslavia.
"We can assume that the Social Democrats will lose their majority but the question is how much will their vote drop," Beutelmeyer said. "The Freedom Party will make moderate gains".
The far right is already the second biggest party in the capital, having ousted the conservative People's Party (OeVP) into third place in the last Vienna elections in 1991.
The OeVP is the junior partner in a coalition with the Social Democrats (SPOe) at federal government level.
After Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl is the second most powerful figure in the SPOe.
Haeupl signalled he would resign if Social Democrat support dropped below 40 percent, as predicted by some voter surveys.
"That would certainly be a dramatic situation that may have repercussions at national level," Beutelmeyer said.
In the 1991 Vienna elections, the Social Democrats won 52 of 100 seats in city hall. The latest opinion polls put support for the party around 40 percent, down from 48 percent then.
The Freedom Party is riding high in the polls with around 26 percent support, up from 23 percent in 1991.
For the Social Democrats, losing their grip on power in Vienna would come as a shock in a city they regard as the showcase for party policy.

The state's 133 billion schilling ($12.34 billion) spending budget dwarfs every other region. Health spending alone -- at 30 billion schillings annually -- is bigger than the entire budget for the southern province of Styria.
A huge home-building programme means about a quarter of all Vienna's flats are publicly-owned. And hundreds of thousands of Viennese are employed directly or indirectly by the council.
As an example of the power the council wields, Vienna city hall indirectly controls Austria's biggest bank, Bank Austria.
Despite voter dissatisfaction, the capital is among the safest cities in Europe and unemployment, though above the national average of 4.1 percent, is still low by EU standards.
"In purely financial terms the city is in good health," said Peter Mayerhofer of economic research institute WIFO.
Vienna council says it will meet financial targets set by central government and expects to beat its own deficit goal of 13 billion schillings by three billion this year. ($1=10.78 Schilling)
